Open with the business problem, before introducing graph neural networks. A payment-monitoring team sees many legitimate transfers and a small number of potentially illicit ones. It must decide which events deserve review. This project examines one information-design choice: are counts of an account’s activity sufficient, or should the model also know the history of the particular sender–receiver pair? The experiment concerns transaction classification in synthetic labelled data. It does not evaluate an entire AML programme or make a production deployment recommendation. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
Explain AML as anti-money-laundering monitoring: payments can be examined individually and in their wider transaction network. A model score is an input to an investigation process, not a legal determination. In this benchmark, a true positive is a flagged transaction with a synthetic laundering label; a false positive is a flagged transaction without that label. Business teams care about both missed activity and the demand placed on investigators. F1 is a useful research summary, but the same F1 can arise from different alert volumes. Later we therefore show the underlying transaction counts. A transaction flag is not necessarily a unique case, customer investigation, or suspicious activity report. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
Use the two simple networks as an introductory example. A repeated customer–supplier relationship and a distribution across multiple recipients can have the same number of transfers. Distinct-counterparty counts separate these patterns, which makes them a plausible simple explanation for gains attributed to graph adaptations. However, even after we know how many counterparties an account has used, we may still not know whether the current recipient is one of them. Fan-in and fan-out are structural motifs discussed in the multigraph literature; this study does not estimate separate performance for each laundering typology. Do not label either illustrative network as inherently suspicious. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
Define a counterparty as the account on the other side of a transfer. The four count features summarize the sender’s outgoing history and the receiver’s incoming history. Ports are local numerical ranks assigned when a counterparty is first encountered and reused on later transfers. They are unrelated to network communication ports and are not KYC identities or globally unique customer IDs. An explicit novelty bit says whether this sender has previously transferred to this receiver in the observed history. This distinction is central: an account can be established while the relationship is first observed. Features are limited by the observation window; unobserved earlier relationships can look new. Introduce the source before model details. We downloaded the specified IBM AML HI-Small dataset, pinned its revision, and verified the archive checksum. It has 5,078,345 transfers involving 515,088 accounts, with 5,177 laundering labels. Severe class imbalance means that predicting every transaction as legitimate would have high accuracy while detecting no laundering, which is why we focus on minority-class F1 and average precision. Accounts are identified by bank and account ID. The synthetic data offer labels for controlled comparisons, but do not substitute for an evaluation of real investigators’ dispositions or real customer harm. All endpoint, label, and historical-feature alignments were independently audited. Explain why temporal separation is relevant to monitoring: the model should be assessed on a later period rather than an arbitrary mixture of the same days. Whole-day boundaries prevent an exact 60/20/20 allocation. The late test tail is unusual: its prevalence is 59.12%, compared with 0.111% on test days 8–9. A retrospective rule flagging everything from day 10 would score 48.18 full-test F1. We do not present that rule as a deployable detector because it was noticed after inspecting test data. Instead, the full test remains primary and days 8–9 form a disclosed sensitivity. Temporal splitting alone does not make this a live chronological simulation: evaluation graph construction still uses the cumulative period. Introduce a GNN in one sentence: it learns account representations by combining information from neighboring accounts and transactions. Xu et al. motivate the GIN architecture; their work is not an AML result. Altman et al. provide the labelled synthetic financial environment. Egressy et al. show that local port numbering improves a directed multigraph GNN on HI-Small and connect it to distinguishing repeated edges and distinct neighbors. The reported 28.70 to 54.85 result motivates our question, but our five-epoch protocol has scoring and ordering differences and is not a numerical replication. The gap is explanatory: a port may help partly because it exposes counts or relationship novelty, rather than because a model needs a richer counterparty-rank signal. We test that explanation directly. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
State the competing explanation clearly. A port on a first contact equals the number of distinct partners previously encountered at that endpoint. Perhaps much of its benefit can be replaced by basic account counters. If so, the additional gain from ports should shrink once those counters are available. The factorial design tests this attenuation, rather than comparing Counts alone with Ports alone. The supplementary novelty cell asks whether making current-pair membership explicit is a useful alternative representation. This is a feature-design question with operational relevance, but the experiment does not compare GNNs with rule systems or tabular models, so it cannot establish that a GNN is necessary. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
Explain the 2×2 visually before the equation. The four core cells have base transaction attributes in common: elapsed timestamp, received amount, receiving currency, and payment format. The count factors add four prefix-history values. The port factor adds incoming and outgoing first-contact ranks. Five paired random seeds are used across every cell, with fixed hyperparameters and five epochs. The fifth cell replaces ports with a novelty bit alongside counts. Counts, ports, and novelty use one total order: timestamp and a fixed random tie-break within a minute. Earlier means earlier in this convention, not a claimed true intraminute ordering. We completed all planned runs without extending the budget based on final results. Here B_s, P_s, C_s, and CP_s denote seed-specific test F1 for Base, Ports, Counts, and Counts+Ports. Overbars denote means across the five paired seeds. Explain the estimand in words first: if counts are the explanation, the additional benefit of ports should become smaller. Use a ratio of mean paired differences, not the average of seed-wise ratios. Each epoch’s decision threshold maximizes validation F1 and is then applied unchanged to test. Primary selection uses the best validation F1 among zero-based epochs 1–4, with earliest ties. No test outcome chooses the epoch or threshold. The intervals describe variation across five training/scoring seeds conditional on this dataset and protocol; they do not estimate uncertainty across banks. The ratio needs Fieller inference because denominator uncertainty matters. Final-epoch, early-test, and AP views are disclosed sensitivities. The analysis was refined with inherited interim results available, not preregistered outcome-blind. Present the directly interpretable differences before the negative ratio. Ports add 7.48 F1 points without the counters, and 14.91 points after counters are supplied. Their respective paired intervals are [2.96,12.00] and [10.11,19.71]. The requested explained share is −99.35% with Fieller interval [−512.75%,+8.42%]. Under the stated model, large positive attenuation is incompatible with the results, whereas zero attenuation and substantial amplification remain possible. Do not say that ports have proven to become twice as valuable: the interaction interval includes zero. Counts alone shows an imprecise gain, but that does not mean counts are useless. This finding is about substitution within this five-epoch GIN experiment. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
Connect the finding back to the introductory questions. The supplementary novelty representation outperforms counts plus ranks in every seed. Its advantage is concentrated among first-contact transactions. This does not mean every new relationship should trigger an alert: most first-contact transfers are legitimate even in this synthetic test set. Nor does it prove that ranks never help. CP versus CN replaces a rank representation with an explicit bit; it does not test adding ranks to a model that already has explicit novelty. A model may learn the explicit bit more easily than infer it from normalized counts and ranks in five epochs. Ports are local ranks, not global customer identities. Appendix B explains why the first-contact determinism argument does not imply a zero gain. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
This is the main business translation. The whole test set contains 863,900 transfers and 1,611 labelled positives. Moving from counts to counts plus ports improves both detection and false positives at the selected thresholds. Moving from counts plus ports to explicit novelty finds still more positives, but increases the total number of flags. It would therefore be misleading to sell the novelty result as lower workload. All entries are arithmetic means across seeds; each actual run has integer counts. Different models have different validation-selected thresholds, so these are not comparisons at equal alert volume or false-positive rate. Real AML teams group transactions into cases, assign varying review effort, and use information outside this benchmark. We did not measure case yield, investigator hours, suspicious activity reporting, prevented loss, or return on investment. Do not claim three independent confirmations: these views reuse the same models and dataset, and the additional checks were motivated by interim results and the tail. The early-test comparison removes the unusual late-period transactions. Final validation AP concerns a period without that test tail and assesses ranking rather than one cutoff, although validation has also informed model selection. The residual and novelty advantages have positive intervals in these views. Counterevidence remains important: the original port gain on final test AP has an interval crossing zero, and at a fixed 0.5 threshold the primary residual-gain interval also crosses zero. The conclusion applies to the specified validation-calibrated protocol, not every possible threshold. Locate the importance at the right decision level. A feature-engineering or model-risk team should not assume that aggregate counters preserve all useful relationship context. An explicit first-observed-pair feature deserves careful testing because it is effective here and has a clear meaning. But a simple model input does not guarantee inexpensive infrastructure: maintaining pair history requires identity resolution, an observation window, data completeness, and state storage. A production validation should construct features and message-passing neighborhoods only from information actually available at scoring time, normalize from training data, and evaluate later periods. Compare models at a common review capacity, then measure case-level outcomes if available. Training convergence is unestablished: 23 of 25 chosen checkpoints were the last epoch. None of these follow-up studies has been completed in this experiment. Presentation design: displayed figures are rendered in Python and inserted as images; detailed caveats remain in these notes.
Close in the same vocabulary used at the beginning. We started with frequency, breadth, and the current relationship. The experiment shows that the specified frequency and breadth counts do not remove the value of ports. The novelty comparison points to a useful, explicit representation of current-pair history at this budget. That is the original contribution: testing and constraining an explanation, rather than simply repeating a published performance ranking. Keep the scope in the final spoken sentence: these are results on a synthetic dataset, with five-epoch GIN training and transductive scoring. They justify focused feature validation, not an identity-causation claim or immediate deployment. Direct the audience to the report, all five seed results, code, and audits. For a technical question, define D and N as mean seed contrasts and I=N−D. Then S=−I/D. The original port-gain interval is positive, so the Fieller set is bounded. Zero explained share corresponds to I=0 and remains compatible; complete explanation corresponds to N=0 and is excluded. The asymmetric interval contains useful information about attenuation even though amplification is very imprecise. Inference assumes independent seed blocks and approximately normal paired differences on one fixed dataset. These five seeds are not independent financial populations. Do not substitute the paper’s 26.15-point gain into our denominator, clip the estimate to 0–100%, or call the ratio a causal identity fraction. The count tuple lists sender total, sender distinct, receiver total, and receiver distinct, in that order. This small counterexample clarifies the mechanism and prevents overclaiming. The raw count vector is identical for all three alternatives. A port equals its corresponding distinct count on a first contact and is lower on a repeat, so counts plus ports can reveal novelty. Equality holds conditional on group membership; it is not a global function of counts alone. A pooled predictor can therefore improve on first contacts when ports help it identify the group. Neighboring repeated edges create another route through which GNN messages can carry rank information. This example concerns the raw features, not an impossibility theorem for full graphs. The observed comparison with explicit novelty does not isolate rank after novelty; a future sixth cell would do so.
